client: I've been feeling really off ever since Maria and I broke up about three months ago. Things I used to love, like going hiking with my friends on weekends, just don't feel the same anymore — I go sometimes, but I'm kind of just going through the motions. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change how I feel, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: It takes real courage to show up even when you're not sure it'll help, and I'm really glad you gave this a shot. It sounds like the breakup has left things feeling a bit flat and hollow — like the color has faded from things that used to bring you joy, even when you're physically doing them. I'm curious, when you're out on those hikes and going through the motions, what kinds of thoughts tend to run through your mind?

client: Honestly, a lot of it is just... I keep thinking about things Maria and I used to do together, like there were certain trails we'd hike and now I can't stop comparing everything to how it was with her. And then I start feeling guilty, like maybe I'm ruining it for my friends because I'm not really present, or I wonder if they even notice how checked out I am. It's kind of exhausting to be surrounded by people and still feel completely alone.
therapist: That feeling of being surrounded by people yet still feeling completely alone is such a heavy thing to carry, and it makes a lot of sense given how much those trails and moments are tied to memories of Maria. I also notice you're being pretty hard on yourself — jumping to worry that you're somehow letting your friends down, even as you're clearly going through something really painful. I'm wondering, is there any evidence your friends actually feel that way, or is that more of a fear your mind is generating?

client: I mean, no, my friends haven't actually said anything like that — they keep inviting me, so I guess that's something. But it's hard to just dismiss the fear because it feels so real in the moment, like my gut is telling me something even if the facts don't back it up. And honestly, even if they don't notice, I notice, and that almost makes it worse — like I'm failing at something I used to be good at.
therapist: You're actually doing something really important right now — you're able to see that the facts and the feeling don't fully line up, even if the feeling still has a strong grip on you, and that kind of awareness is genuinely a skill. What strikes me is this idea of "failing at something you used to be good at" — it sounds like you're holding yourself to a standard of how you *used* to show up, without much room for the fact that you're grieving. I'm curious, if a close friend told you they were going through a breakup and struggling to be present on hikes, would you see them as failing?

client: No, obviously I wouldn't see them as failing — I'd probably tell them it makes complete sense and to cut themselves some slack. But when I try to apply that same logic to myself it just... doesn't land the same way, like I know intellectually it should work but it feels hollow or like I'm just telling myself what I want to hear. I'm not sure why it's so much easier to be kind to someone else than to myself.
therapist: What you're describing is really common, and the fact that you can see the double standard so clearly is actually meaningful progress — your mind isn't fully buying its own harsh verdict. That gap between *knowing* something and *feeling* it is real, and it's not a sign the logic is wrong; it just means the self-critical voice has had a lot more practice than the compassionate one. What do you think that inner critic is trying to protect you from, if anything — like, what might it be afraid would happen if you actually did cut yourself some slack?

client: That's a question I haven't really thought about before, and sitting with it for a second... I think maybe the critic is afraid that if I go easy on myself, I'll just wallow in it and never actually move forward. Like if I stop pushing myself to show up and perform normally, I'll just sink into the grief and lose momentum completely. It's almost like the self-criticism is the thing keeping me functional, even if it doesn't feel great.
therapist: That's a really profound insight — you've essentially uncovered the hidden logic behind the critic, that it believes it's the engine keeping you going, even while it's quietly exhausting you. It's worth gently questioning that assumption though: is there any evidence in your life that self-compassion leads to wallowing, or might it actually be that the constant self-pressure is part of what's draining the joy from those hikes in the first place? What would "moving forward" even look like to you, if it didn't have to involve pushing yourself so hard?

client: Honestly, I can't think of a time where being kind to myself actually made me give up on something — so maybe the critic's logic doesn't really hold up under scrutiny. But I'm struggling to even picture what moving forward without the self-pressure looks like, because I've kind of operated this way for so long that it feels like just... who I am. I guess part of me worries that if I let go of that, I won't recognize myself anymore.
therapist: You've just done something really significant — you tested the critic's core belief and found it doesn't actually hold up, which takes honesty and courage. That fear of not recognizing yourself without the self-pressure is so understandable, but I'd gently offer that what you're describing sounds less like your identity and more like a coping strategy you picked up somewhere along the way — one that may have served you once but is now costing you more than it gives. I'm curious, when you imagine a version of yourself that moves through grief with more kindness rather than pressure, what's one small word or quality that comes to mind for who that person might be?

client: The word that comes to mind is "patient," but even as I say it, it feels a little foreign, like I'm describing someone else rather than myself. I think I've spent so long equating patience with weakness or giving up that it's hard to claim it as something positive. But maybe that's exactly the problem — I've had the whole thing backwards this whole time.
therapist: That moment of "I've had the whole thing backwards" is a genuinely meaningful shift, and even if it feels quiet and a little uncertain right now, those kinds of realizations have a way of slowly reshaping how we see ourselves. Patience isn't giving up — it's actually what allows real healing to happen without forcing it, and it sounds like some part of you already knows that, even if it feels foreign to claim. I'm wondering, is there one small moment this week — maybe on a hike or just in a quiet moment — where you could practice treating patience as a strength rather than a weakness, and just notice what that feels like?

client: I like the idea in theory, but I'm a little worried that in the moment I'll just default back to the old pattern without even realizing it — like the self-criticism is so automatic that I won't catch it until I'm already deep in it. Maybe I could try it on the hike this weekend, just notice when I start comparing myself to how I used to be and see if I can pause instead of piling on. But I'm not making any promises, because I've tried to "just notice things" before and it kind of fizzled out pretty quickly.
therapist: It's really honest and self-aware of you to name that worry upfront, and the fact that you're not making grand promises actually shows good judgment rather than pessimism. The automatic nature of self-criticism is real — it's had years of practice — so rather than trying to catch it before it starts, what if the goal this weekend was simply to notice it *at some point* during the hike, even if you're already deep in it, and just gently name it without judgment? I'm curious, what would feel like a small but genuine "win" to you after that hike on Sunday?

client: I think a genuine win would just be getting to the end of the hike and not feeling worse about myself than when I started — like, not leaving with that heavy feeling that I failed at being present. That feels like a pretty low bar when I say it out loud, but honestly right now it doesn't feel low at all, it feels like something I'd actually have to work for. Maybe that's okay though, maybe that's where I'm starting from and that's just the reality of it.
therapist: That's not a low bar at all — that's an honest, grounded place to start from, and there's real wisdom in meeting yourself where you actually are rather than where you think you should be. "This is where I'm starting from" is not defeat; it's actually the foundation that makes real progress possible, and it sounds like some part of you is beginning to make peace with that. As you head into this week, I'm wondering — is there someone in your life, maybe one of those friends on the hike, you'd feel comfortable leaning on just a little, even without having to explain everything?

client: There's one friend, Jake, who I think kind of senses something is off with me even though I haven't said much — he's checked in a couple of times in a low-key way that didn't feel like pressure. But I get uncomfortable with the idea of leaning on him because I don't want to make the hike about my stuff or become that person who brings the whole mood down. I guess I'm not sure there's a middle ground between saying nothing and making it a whole thing.
therapist: It sounds like Jake might already be offering you a quiet open door, and the fact that he's checked in without pressure suggests he can probably handle more than you're giving him credit for. That "all or nothing" thinking — either say nothing or make it a whole thing — is worth noticing, because there's actually a lot of space in between, like simply saying "I've been going through something lately, but I'm glad to be out here" and letting that be enough. What do you think would happen if Jake knew just a little more than he does now?
